title: Points of interest
attributionIntro: Every photograph here is freely licensed. Crediting the author is a condition of CC BY and CC BY-SA, not a courtesy. Material without a free licence is not included in the app.

cupola-oculus.title: Cupola and oculus
cupola-oculus.text: A shallow stone cupola. Not every vault is pierced, and the ones that are do not line up: three openings in eight storeys, over storeys 1, 4 and 7, so there is no view of the sky from the bottom of the tower. The marker hangs under the widest of them, in storey 4 — Ø about 2.4 m, read off the walkthrough footage against the glass guard ring around the hole, ±0.5 m. Storey 1's opening is the well the modern steel spiral climbs through, not an oculus. The shape of the vault itself is still an assumption: no source gives the rise of these domes.

well.title: The well
well.text: A 0.7 m bore, 21 m deep to the aquifer. The mouth is wider than the bore — a funnel clearly visible in the photograph — which is why 0.7 m is taken as the bore and not as the opening in the floor. Sources disagree on the storey: the project reference says the second, while the photographer's caption and İçərişəhər say the third.

staircase.title: Stair in the wall thickness
staircase.text: The flight runs inside the masonry, abutting the inner circle. The winding was read from photographs — counterclockwise when ascending, though the work plan had assumed the opposite. No source gives step dimensions, so riser and going are chosen so that each flight lands exactly on the next floor.

passage-slit.title: Slit at a stair landing
passage-slit.text: Narrow outside, flaring inward. This is an aperture for admitting a beam, not a sector for viewing: a slit in this wall accepts light only within a few degrees of its own axis. It opens off the landing at the end of a stair passage rather than off a chamber — the owner, who has walked the building, states that the storeys themselves have no windows at all and that the openings are only at the beginning and the end of the stair passages. So the reveal stops at the passage wall, about 2.7 m in, not at the room face. The inner dimensions are still not measured: the single interior photograph gives proportion, not metres. Which landings actually carry one is not settled either. He says some flights have a window at the beginning of the climb and at the end, others at one end only — and nobody has yet asked him flight by flight, so the model falls back on a geometric test and marks the answer as missing rather than guessing it.

slits.title: Slit windows from outside
slits.text: Eight slits are countable on the photographed face, in two columns of four. The lower four hold one bearing to within 1.1° — a true vertical generator; the upper four stand about 35° round from them, drift a further 15° as they descend, and lie entirely above the lower ones, so no two slits share a height anywhere. The owner, who has walked the building, pointed at this very frame and said: «на настоящей башне окна если смотреть с переди клюва находятся с левой стороны клюва в таком вот распорядке и отдалении друг от друга» — on the real tower the windows, seen from in front of the beak, are on the LEFT of it, in this arrangement and at this spacing. So he endorses the photographed pattern, and the model does not reproduce it. The disagreements are measured rather than tuned away: nine openings against eight; columns 97° apart against 35 ± 4°, re-measured on two frames with a sine instead of a linear pixel scale; eight rungs against six levels, with a gap in the model twice its own pitch — where the 4→6 flight passes storey 5 without ending — and two more photographed slits inside it. The pitch itself does NOT disagree — see below. The sharpest of them is visible from his own viewpoint: standing in front of the beak, the model shows two openings to its left and both hug the pier, one opening to its RIGHT, and six that lie past the drum's tangent point where no distance can bring them into view. The quarter turn he gave earlier the same day lands exactly on that tangent point. What could reconcile his two answers is listed in src/data/windows.json → reconciliation and the question he must answer is beside it in beakSideQuestion; no geometry has been changed. Which flight ends carry a window is still his to say — he has not been asked end by end, and the model is standing in with a check on whether daylight could reach each one at all. One thing did close, and by changing the ruler rather than the model: measured DOWN FROM THE CROWN in drum radii — a unit neither side has to borrow a ground line for — the eight photographed slits stand one per storey, six of them landing on a model landing within half a metre, and the pitch between them agrees to about 20 mm. The 2.8-against-3.3 m gap is an artefact of the vertical datum: fitting the drum's top rim arc in three frames puts its visible foot on the beak side 4.2–4.4 radii below the crown, which is 35 m at the documented 16.5 m diameter against 29.5 m of documented height, and the two do not fit together on this face. What is left is horizontal, and sharper for it: the photographed bearing does not drift from one column to the other, it steps once — 43° in the single rung between storey 4 and storey 5, which is the storey the owner himself describes as reached from the middle of one long climb. ONE ESCAPE ROUTE CLOSED TODAY WITHOUT ASKING ANYBODY ANYTHING. Stacked flights of equal rise do not put their far ends in a vertical line: the wall thins upward, the walking line moves out, and the same climb sweeps less arc higher up. The lean of that column is the sweep times the taper — and the tread, the riser and the walking radius all cancel out of that ratio, verified by re-planning the whole stair over a 2.4-fold range of sweep. So the lean measures the sweep. The photographed upper column leans 5.1° per storey, which needs a sweep near 176°; a 35° sweep would lean 1.0°. The reading that would have made the two columns the two ends of the same flights — a steeper stair on a shorter tread — is refuted by the same photograph it was drawn from, five times over, with no tread dimension involved. It does not rescue the model either, and that is said in the same breath: its own flights lean 2.3–3.1° per storey. Both readings are wrong on that quantity, one by a factor of two and the other by five. What the model does reproduce is the lower column — feet all begin at one bearing, so a foot column is a true vertical, 0.30° per storey against the 0.3–0.9 photographed. Two corrections belong here as well: two fifths of the model's 97° is not the climb at all but the two end landings and a rule holding each opening clear of the last tread, so the earlier claim that the separation had no free parameters was untrue — though stripping both still leaves 64° against 35. And the sharpest thing left is a question for him rather than a measurement: no two slits share a height anywhere on this face, which flights pierced at BOTH ends cannot produce, so which end of each passage carries a window is now the first thing to ask him. src/data/windows.json → sweepDriftCoupling and → askInThisOrder.

entrance.title: The entrance
entrance.text: The entrance faces west. The project reference said south-east, but the photographs disprove it: in the frame where the door faces the camera the 10.7 m buttress is absent entirely, which is only possible from the opposite bearing. The south-east door of the literature is a different opening, higher up the tower.

buttress.title: The buttress
buttress.text: The beak-shaped projection was measured from the OpenStreetMap footprint: a 3.0 m nose, 10.7 m of projection, an axis at 106.7°, skewed 13.6° off the middle of its own root — hence the asymmetric flanks. The texts call the direction east, but the measurement gives 106.7°, which is 16.6° away from equinox sunrise.

section.title: The section drawing
section.text: A redraw of a 1980 book plate. It agrees with the model on eight domed chambers, a stair in the wall and the well shaft, but it carries no scale bar, so not one number in the model comes from it. Where it parts company is the middle: the plate draws a coaxial oculus in every vault, while the 2026 walkthrough finds three pierced vaults and no common axis, and the model follows the footage. It also shows the inner chamber offset from the axis, which the model does not yet reproduce.
